subject: Linking two different single items in a longitudinal study

messages.author: 3a176c26aaba8d2d
messages.subject: Linking two different single items in a longitudinal study
parts:
Hi Phil,

thank you for answering my previous question. I now have a completely different one: I have the situation where a group of people where asked a single item for a trait at T1 and then another item (comparable to the first item but slightly different wording and more importantly with a different scale, but still a measure for the same trait). 

I now want to assess whether people increased/decreased there scores from T1 to T2, so I need to make the two items comparable. I am running the model below (based on code from this forum) but the confidence intervals of the parameters are very wide and the condition number of the information matrix is 1680039. I am freeing the second mean because that's what I'm interested in (compared to MEAN1 which is 0).

Is this the correct way to go or am I simply trying something that is not possible? I also fitted a model without constraining the loadings to 1, but the condition number is even higher. Hope you can help!

Best, Dirk

model2 <- 'Time1 = 1
          Time2 = 2
          START = (1,a1,1.0),(2,a2,1.0)
          FIXED = (1,a1),(2,a2)
          COV = Time1*Time2
          MEAN = Time2'

messages.author: b330c2028fed415b
messages.subject: Re: Linking two different single items in a longitudinal study
parts:
Hi Dirk,

The high condition number makes sense since this model is not identified, so it's good that it was picked up in the final model (stochastic algorithms can still converge to something, but it's likely not meaningful or even unique). If you want to free the Time2 mean, and given your hypothesized structure, then I think you should try to set equality constraints for the intercepts between as many items across the tests as possible. At least one intercept needs to be constrained in the second way to make this model identified, but to obtain a stable estimate the more the better. 

Basically, the idea is to force a set of items to remain equally difficult over time so that systematic changes at the latent variable level can be made in reference to this baseline information. Without this constraint it wouldn't be clear if, for instance, the individual latent trait values increased over time, the items just got easier in the second round, or both (hence, the lack of identifiability regarding the source of change). HTH.

Phil
